lines.text: How do hackers stay invisible online? It's not magic. It's layers.
Every time you go online, you leave a trail. Your IP address is like a return address on every message you send.
Your browser has a fingerprint too: your screen, your fonts, your settings. And a photo can carry the exact spot where it was taken.
A VPN hides your address from the website. But the VPN company can see it, so you're really just moving your trust.
Tor goes further. Your message is wrapped in three layers of encryption, like an onion, and bounced through three computers.
Each one peels off one layer. The first knows who you are, but not where you're going. The last knows where you're going, but not who you are.
So how do people still get caught? Almost never by the math. By one small mistake: a reused username, a logged-in account, a photo with location on.
That's the idea behind Orbi Transfer. No account, no email, no name. Just a nickname, if you want one.
Your file is locked in your browser with your code. The code never leaves your phone, so even our server can't open it.
We keep a scrambled fingerprint of your network, never the address itself. Want a room just for your crew? Make a private space.
And 30 minutes later, the file burns.
